events/1265_firenze/phases/0/narrative: 1373, Florence, the church of Santo Stefano. The first “Dante lectures” in history begin — the speaker: Giovanni Boccaccio.
events/1265_firenze/phases/0/instruction: Click Boccaccio at the lectern and hear him begin.
events/1265_firenze/phases/0/npcs/0/dial: In 1265, under the sign of Gemini, a baby was born in this city.
Fifty years later, the same city sentenced him to burn.
Today the city pays me to talk about him. My friends — let's start at the beginning.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/title: Outside the Baptistery of San Giovanni
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/narrative: May 1265, Florence. A son is born to the Alighieri. They name him Durante — for short, Dante.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/instruction: Walk around the market outside the Baptistery and hear what the city is saying.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: Here a guild's banner counts for more than a lord's sword. That's Florence.
Wool cloth, banks, spices — we live on trade, not on castles.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: Five years ago, Montaperti. The Ghibellines came back at us with Siena's troops…
The water of the Arbia ran red.
The emperor's party, the pope's party — a child born in this city has to pick a side.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: The Alighieri? Minor nobles, Guelphs — that's the pope's party.
They say that while she was carrying him, his mother dreamed she gave birth under a laurel tree.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/3/dial: See that eight-sided baptistery? San Giovanni — our “beautiful St John.”
The font inside — every child in this city starts there.
events/1265_firenze/phases/1/npcs/4/dial: The eight-sided Baptistery stands in the middle of the square, its marble walls bright in the morning light. Next spring, on Holy Saturday, the baby called Dante will be baptised here along with all the city's newborns.
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/prompt: His great-great-grandfather is telling his own life. Put it back in order.
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/1/ca: A woman at her spindle, telling stories
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/2/ca: A wife from the Po valley
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/panels/3/ca: He rides off under the cross
events/1265_firenze/phases/2/revealNote:
A city, a household, a marriage, a crusade — and it all lands on one baby.
He isn't telling history. He's telling where this child comes from.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/narrative: At the lectern, Boccaccio opens Paradiso XV — Dante's great-great-grandfather Cacciaguida, the crusader martyr, remembering the old, plain Florence.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/instruction: Click the picture and go panel by panel.
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/0/di: “Florence, inside her old walls, lived plain and quiet. The bells rang for morning and midday prayer, the way they always had.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/1/di: “The mothers kept to spindle and thread, and by the cradle told the old stories — Troy, Fiesole and Rome.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/2/di: “My wife came from the Po valley. Your family name — Alighieri — came from her.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/3/di: “Then I followed the Emperor Conrad on crusade, and died for the faith in the Holy Land. From that death I came to this peace.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/3/panels/4/di: Holy Saturday, the next spring. The baby is baptised in the Baptistery of San Giovanni and named Durante Alighieri.
“Out of my blood will come a man who walks through all three realms.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/narrative: Nine years pass. The Alighieri boy grows up among parchment and copied books. His mother died young; his father makes a small living lending money.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/instruction: Click the things in the study, and the family.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/0/dial: A copy of the Aeneid lies open on the desk — the epic of Virgil of Mantua. The margins are covered in a boy's clumsy notes.
This man from Mantua… my teacher.
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/1/dial: A dusty spindle stands in the corner. His mother Bella died when he was small.
…Was the dream under the laurel tree true, mother?
events/1265_firenze/phases/4/npcs/2/dial: Reading again? Fine. For a small house like ours, the pen is safer than the sword.
There's a feast tomorrow at a great house. You're coming with me. Wear something decent.
events/1265_firenze/phases/5/transitionT:
In May of his ninth year, at a feast, he saw a girl in a crimson dress.
Later he wrote:
“Behold, a god stronger than I, who comes to rule over me.”
events/1265_firenze/phases/5/announcemen: Boccaccio: “My friends, remember that crimson dress. What a nine-year-old felt that day will grow into the biggest poem in the Christian world.”
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/question: In the Florence where Dante was born, which two parties made the deepest political split?
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/options/1: The Guelphs (the pope's party) and the Ghibellines (the emperor's party)
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/0/explanation: In the 13th century Italy was split between the Guelphs, who backed the pope, and the Ghibellines, who backed the Holy Roman Emperor. At Montaperti in 1260 the Ghibellines used Siena's army to crush Florence's Guelphs. The Whites and the Blacks came later — a split inside the Guelphs themselves.
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/1/question: In Paradiso XV, which ancestor tells Dante about the “old, plain Florence”?
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/1/explanation: Cacciaguida is Dante's great-great-grandfather. He went on the Second Crusade with the Emperor Conrad III and died fighting. In Paradiso XV–XVII he remembers the old city and foretells Dante's exile. The name Alighieri came from his wife.
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/2/question:
After nine-year-old Dante first saw Beatrice, he wrote:
“Behold, a god ___ than I, who comes to rule over me”
quiz/1265_firenze/quizzes/2/explanation: From chapter two of the Vita Nuova. At a feast, nine-year-old Dante saw Beatrice for the first time, and from then on “the god of love ruled my soul” — and that feeling grew, in the end, into the Divine Comedy.
